about: session-harvest is the only skill in this corpus with an inverted invocation profile: 13 auto
against 87 explicit, where plan-docs runs 70 against 15. That split is behavioural, not lexical
- a person typing /name is a person the description did not serve - which makes it the one
pointer at a description problem that survived a day of failed lexical heuristics.
It is not proof of one. The description opens 'Use when invoked explicitly as /session-harvest',
so some of that 87 is the skill working as designed. The description ALSO lists auto-trigger
phrasings, and whether those fire has never been tested.
So the suite is built as a controlled comparison rather than a pass/fail:
cases 1-2  the description's own listed phrasings, quoted almost verbatim. These are the
control. If they fail, the problem is severe and lexical.
cases 3-6  the same need in a person's words, two of them lifted from real transcripts in
this store where the user typed a command afterwards.
cases 7-8  the nearest neighbour, plan-docs, whose territory session-harvest's description
names directly (plans/*.md, AGENTS.md).
cases 9-10 ordinary requests that touch session-harvest's vocabulary - commits, pushes, CI -
and should fire nothing at all.
A control that passes while the paraphrases fail isolates the variable exactly: the description
works on its own wording and not on the request's.
RESULT 2026-08-31: 10/10, precision 1.0 for both skills. The controls passed 3/3 AND so did
every paraphrase, including both phrasings lifted from real transcripts. Nothing fired on the
two should-not-trigger cases, despite session-harvest's description naming commits, pushes and
CI. plan-docs kept its own two cases.
So 13-auto-against-87-explicit is NOT a description defect. The description opens 'Use when
invoked explicitly as /session-harvest' and the auto-trigger phrasings it lists all work; the
split is the skill behaving as designed plus a person's habit of typing it. The rule that sent
us here - high explicit and low auto means a description problem - is a hypothesis worth a
suite, and on its first test it was wrong.
